title: The Starry Night
teaser: A swirling sky, painted from memory in an asylum room.

lesson.text: June 1889. Vincent van Gogh is 36. A month earlier, he checked himself into the asylum at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, after a severe breakdown in Arles.
His room faces east. Through the window he sees a wheat field, the Alpilles hills and, before dawn, the sky. He paints it more than twenty times, at every hour.
Here is the most famous of those skies. Take in the whole painting, then tap to step inside.

spots.title: The swirl
spots.text: At the center, two great waves coil into each other. No sky looks like this: he paints what he feels, not what he sees.

spots.title: The moon
spots.text: An orange crescent in a yellow halo: it almost looks like a sun. Van Gogh lays the paint in short strokes that circle around it.

spots.title: The morning star
spots.text: The whitest star in the painting. Van Gogh wrote to his brother that he had seen the morning star, very large, before sunrise. It is most likely Venus.

lesson.text: This painting wasn't made at night, or in front of the scene. Van Gogh painted it by day, in his studio at the asylum, from memory and imagination. That was unusual for him: he usually painted what was right in front of his eyes.
The Starry Night was painted by day, from memory. It isn't a view, it's a vision.
